title: The rabbi's son
hook: another tale: a son is kept from his true teacher by his father's doubts until too late
tomorrow: what if someone argued your case to heaven, every single time?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven beggars, each flaw opening on a gift, the seventh day still untold. The hidden gift. Today, another of Rebbe Nachman's tales, and a harder one.

A tab stays open on the laptop for weeks: an application, a sign-up, a message never sent. Every week brings a fresh, sensible reason to wait. Rebbe Nachman told a tale about exactly that, and it answers the question plainly. The rabbi's son never reached his teacher because every delay looked reasonable. A rabbi's only son, a gifted student, feels something missing, and longs to travel to a certain tzaddik, a holy teacher. His father doubts the man. Still, they set out.
screen: `A TAB OPEN FOR WEEKS.` → `A SON WHO FEELS SOMETHING MISSING.` → `A FATHER WHO DOUBTS.`

segments.voice: On the first trip the horses stumble and the wagon tips. The father says: a sign from heaven. They turn back. On the next try an axle breaks. Another sign. On the third, at an inn, a merchant says he knows the tzaddik, and speaks of him with contempt. That settles it. They go home. Here the tale turns dark, so gently: the son falls ill and dies. Later he comes to his father in a dream, burning with anger, and tells him to go. The father goes. At the same inn he meets the same merchant, who now says who he is: the Evil One. He was behind every stumble. The son and the tzaddik, he says, were a lesser light and a greater light, and if they had met, the Messiah would have come. Some readers hear in it how hard the world pushes back on the good things. And it's honest about something ordinary: obstacles aren't always signs. Sometimes they're just obstacles, and the voice calling them signs is the doubt that was already there. The father wasn't wicked. He was careful, a little proud, and slow. That's what makes the tale hurt. It never asks anyone to stop being careful. It asks you to notice when careful has quietly turned into never.
screen: `THE WAGON TIPS: A SIGN?` · `A MERCHANT'S CONTEMPT.` · `THE SON DIES; THE DREAM.` · `THE MERCHANT WAS THE EVIL ONE.` · then, large: `DON'T WAIT TOO LONG.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you keep meaning to do that feels like a calling: a class, a call, a skill, a visit. Name the wish in a few words, then the obstacle that keeps winning, the one that always sounds reasonable. Then shape one small plan for when it shows up again: when that reason comes, I'll take this one step anyway.
The rabbi's son: Rebbe Nachman's tale of a son kept from his teacher by his father's doubts, read as signs, until it was too late.
For today: don't wait too long, because an obstacle isn't always a sign from above. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Rebbe Nachman's tales are read aloud and studied in Breslov circles and beyond; 'The Rabbi and His Only Son' is often taught as a warning against letting doubts, dressed up as signs, keep a person from what calls them.

chat.meaning: Rebbe Nachman's tale warns that obstacles aren't always signs; the father's careful delays cost his son the meeting. Don't wait too long.

notes: For parents: the son in the tale dies. The voice says it in one gentle line ('Here the tale turns dark, so gently: the son falls ill and dies') with no detail.
